The move comes as part of a wider commitment to promote healthy eating and tackle the country's growing childhood obesity crisis. The review will examine current standards and scrutinise the nutritional value of the food served in Scottish schools, with a view to making recommendations for updating the existing nutritional standards for school food. In a bid to reassure the estimated 3.2 million EU citizens living in Britain that they are welcome to remain post-Brexit, Prime Minister Theresa May made a crucial announcement yesterday at the annual Labour Party conference in Brighton. Speaking directly to the anxiety and uncertainty that has been gripping many EU citizens, May divulged her plans to introduce a group of new rights and protections that aim to remove the daunting spectre of uncertainty that has been hovering over the heads of many potential Britons. Prime Minister May stated that it is essential that those individuals who have not merely frequented our shores as weary tourists, but have taken the bold step of making the UK their home, are provided with a sense of security and stability that only long-term residency can offer. The proposed plan promises to give EU citizens – who will be given an "EU Settlement Scheme" – the full range of rights, including the right to work, study, and access to the National Health Service (NHS), as they have enjoyed until now. EU citizens who have built their lives in Britain will be required to register through an online system or at a local authority to secure their status under the new agreement. Once registered, they will have the certainty of a new, settled status, allowing them to stay, study, work, and live in the UK, free from the risk of becoming undocumented. We asked Dr. Polly Conolly, Head of Human Rights for Oxfam, to offer her thoughts on the PM's new plan. "We welcome the Prime Minister's promise that the rights of EU citizens will be protected, but we must ensure that this is more than just a promise. The rights they have had thus far must be enshrined in law, ensuring that the uncertainties of Brexit are alleviated and that these residents can truly feel at home in the UK." An estimated 2 million EU citizens live in low- to modest-income households, meaning that their access to support services and assistance is crucial. Recognition of their residency status is indispensable, not merely to allay their fears but for it also ensures the provision of necessary social services, including access to child benefits, housing help, and assistance with public welfare. It is anticipated that registered free movement citizens will be free to come and go as they please to their home countries, but this 'settled' status guarantees to the EU citizen the ability to live in the UK without additional scrutiny.

It has been 15 years since Dr Andrew Wakefield published research suggesting a possible link between the MMR vaccine and autism, sending shockwaves throughout the nation and sparking a wave of anti-vaccination fervour that has yet to fully recede. Scottish Government Plans Major Overhaul of Organ Donation System In a long-awaited move aimed at reducing waiting times for life-saving transplants, the Scottish Government today published proposals for a new 'soft opt-out' system for organ donation. The publication of the Organ and Tissue Donation (Authorisation) (Scotland) Bill at Holyrood marks a significant shift in the country's approach to the sensitive issue, with the aim of making it easier for Scots to register their consent to donate vital organs after their death. However, those who object to donating will be able to opt-out by registering their decision on a public register. The proposed legislation is the result of an extensive public consultation, with the Scottish Government seeking to balance the need to increase the availability of donated organs with the duty to respect individual autonomy and consent. He said: "For too long, Scotland has been one of the worst-performing countries in Europe when it comes to organ donation. Through this bill, we are seeking to change that by giving those who want to donate the opportunity to do so, and ensuring that the rights of those who object are maintained." Opposition to the soft opt-out system has been expressed by some unionist campaigners, who have argued that such an approach could be seen as ' coercive' and an attack on individual liberty. Embracing the Full Spectrum of Emotions: A Study Reveals the Importance of Authentic Feeling A groundbreaking new study has left researchers and psychologists fascinated by its findings on the power of emotional expression. The research reveals that, contrary to popular wisdom, being able to feel emotions that may be considered unpleasant, such as anger and hatred, is actually a key component of overall happiness and well-being. By exploring the intricate tapestry of human emotions, the study peels back the layers of emotional suppression, suppressing what the researchers describe as a "Western ideal" of merely feeling positive emotions. Published in a leading psychology journal, the research data suggests that individuals who feel the full spectrum of emotions, including the painful and negative ones, report higher levels of life satisfaction and happiness than those who struggle to acknowledge or express these feelings. The study's lead researcher, Dr. Natalia Sarkis, explains that the trend bucks conventional wisdom, which would suggest that the suppression of negative emotions is essential to a fulfilling life. "Our findings indicate that people who can access and navigate their full range of emotions, even the unpleasant ones, exhibit greater emotional intelligence and flexibility," Dr. Sarkis stated. "This capacity to experience and express a wide scope of emotions enables them to navigate life's challenges with greater ease, to connect with others more authentically, and to cultivate a deeper sense of purpose and meaning." The research has far-reaching implications for mental health professionals, educators, and, indeed, society as a whole. Traditionally, therapy and self-help solutions often focus on helping individuals suppress or overcome negative emotions, viewed as debilitating or distressing. However, the study suggests that merely acknowledging and accepting these emotions, rather than attempting to suppress or change them, is the key to unlocking a truer and more authentic emotional experience. "We're not advocating for wallowing in negativity or promulgating self-centered anger or hatred," Dr. Sarkis emphasized. "What we're saying is that it's precisely through embracing and processing our full range of emotions, in all their complexities, that we can create space for deeper connections, empathy, and personal growth." In recognition of the finding that more than 80% of individuals surveyed reported feeling misunderstood or judged for expressing anger or other negative emotions, the researchers stress the importance of creating a culture that acknowledges and validates the full spectrum of human experience. "Cultivating emotional literacy and a greater willingness to engage with our emotions, including the difficult ones, can profoundly enhance our Well-being," Dr. Sarkis said.

Welsh actress Angharad Rees, whose striking beauty and fiery spirit captivated television audiences in the 1970s, has passed away at the age of 63 after a long battle with cancer. With her intense brown eyes, raven-black hair, and piercing gaze, Rees effortlessly brought Demelza to life, effortlessly navigating the character's journey from humble beginnings to a life of societal prominence and marital bliss with Ross. Her captivating performances in the series caught the attention of audiences across Britain and forged a lifelong connection with the programme's fans. Moreover, her acting skills went beyond the confines of Poldark and demonstrated her impressive range as a performer. In the years following Poldark, Rees appeared in various television roles, including romantic dramas such as Harriet's Daughter and Stay Lucky, adding to an impressive filmography that spanned over five decades. Her contributions to British television history have been widely acknowledged and she will always be remembered as one of the most iconic leading ladies of her generation. ScotRail Alliance boss Phil Verster is to step down from his position after 18 months at the helm of the beleaguered rail franchise. It has been a tumultuous period for the ScotRail Alliance, with a seemingly endless series of controversies and disruptions to services dominating the headlines. Yet, despite the numerous challenges the company has faced, Mr Verster has vowed to stay on and see the ScotRail Alliance through its current contract, which comes to an end in March 2025. Sources close to the company have confirmed that Mr Verster will leave once this contract has reached its conclusion, meaning that he will have overseen the ScotRail Alliance through a critical period of transition. His departure has been announced at a time when things could hardly be more difficult for the ScotRail Alliance. The company has faced an onslaught of criticism over the past 18 months, during which time it has struggled to meet its punctuality targets and has been forced to introduce an extraordinary number of engineering works to repair damage to the rail network. Perhaps most pressing of all, however, has been the threat of the ScotRail franchise being re-competed for at the earliest opportunity. This is highly likely to happen if the Scottish government decides not to extend the current contract, as appears increasingly likely. Furthermore, despite Mr Verster's assurances that the ScotRail Alliance is on the verge of a major upgrade, with the introduction of new trains and improved signalling systems, the programme, called ScotRail's "Nyquist" project, is already running significantly behind schedule and substantially over budget. This has sparked fears that the company's transformation is unlikely to be completed in time and that the upgrade may have to be phased. With ongoing problems at FirstGroup, the main operating partner of the ScotRail Alliance and doubts around whether they are fit to continue operating, his decision to move on shows an apparent acceptance that the Alliance needs to refocus and will have to take into a completely new and difficult challenge. Ministers and transport officials have already expressed their gratitude to Mr. Verster for his contribution during his term as boss of the ScotRail Alliance. But it has to be expected that more careful consideration has been given as they've followed this decision with disappointment, because now the biggest challenge ahead seems going to be finding someone equally as well qualified and with a similar background of problems like Mr Verster.

Jungle Legends: The Hidden World of Ancient Monkeys In the dense, mist-shrouded jungles of the Congo Basin, a team of scientists is uncovering a fascinating chapter in the evolution of primates. Primate archaeology, a field that combines primatology with traditional archaeological techniques, has long been considered an esoteric area of study. Yet, the groundbreaking work of researchers like Dr. Elwynn Watts and Dr. Anna Gilardi at Louisiana State University is rewriting the narrative of our primate ancestors. By examining the fossil record, observing modern monkey behaviour, and applying sophisticated dating techniques, primate archaeologists are beginning to reconstruct the lives of ancient monkey societies. What they have discovered is nothing short of astonishing: our distant simian cousins were, it appears, far more complex and resourceful than previously thought. The Kongolo field site in the Diamantina National Park, Republic of Congo, has yielded an extraordinary array of evidence. Excavations have uncovered sophisticated stone tools, crafted from obsidian and quartz, which demonstrate a level of dexterity and cognitive ability hitherto unknown in primate species. Researchers believe that these early monkeys used the tools to crack open nuts and seeds, thereby accessing a rich source of protein and energy in their jungle environment. Moreover, the team has discovered evidence of deliberate funeral practices, with animals deliberately buried with their kin in communal necropoles. This impressive display of cultural sophistication implies that our ancient primate relatives were capable of complex social organisation, compassionate relationships, and – most remarkably – a symbolic understanding of death and the afterlife. Dr. Watts, lead researcher on the project, is effusive in her praise for the early monkeys. "These ancient primates are offering us a glimpse into a world of profound social complexity," she explains. "Their technologies, their ceremonial practices, and even their funerary customs demonstrate a level of cognitive and creative ability that challenges our prevailing assumptions about the evolution of human intelligence." As scientists continue to unravel the mysteries of primate archaeology, we are forced to reevaluate our understanding of the great ape lineage. Our earliest human ancestors, the bipedal Australopithecines, emerge from the fossil record with surprising rapidity – but what about the primates that came before them? Were they merely 'ancestor automatons,' driven by instinct and bloody-minded survival instincts, or did they possess a deep and abiding culture, teeming with clever monkeys who navigated their jungle habitat with aplomb? The discoveries emerging from the Kongolo field site will undoubtedly rewrite the textbooks on primate evolution and inform our understanding of human culture in ways both profound and unexpected.

India's air quality crisis has been a long-standing problem with a huge impact on public health. Every year during the winter months, the rising levels of pollutants in the air envelop the country's cities, posing a significant threat to the health and wellbeing of its citizens. To combat this issue, the Indian government has taken a vital step by launching the country's very first air quality index. This ground-breaking initiative will provide crucial information on pollution levels in real-time, empowering people to make informed decisions about their daily lives. As of today, ten cities in India will be covered under the umbrella of the air quality index, including Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad, Pune, Nagpur, and Lucknow. This number is set to expand to 100 more cities by the end of the year, ensuring that a substantial portion of the population has access to the critical information. According to data from the Union Environment Ministry, there are 22 of the world's most polluted cities in India, which means that more than 100 million people are in constant danger of air pollution-related health problems every day. The ominous effects of the pollution crisis can be clearly seen in statistics - nearly 1,15,000 people in India die prematurely every year due to air pollution. The newly-launched air quality index, modelled on similar systems used by countries like China and Canada, has been developed in collaboration with the US Embassy in Delhi. This system, called the SAFAR (System of Air quality and Flux Analysis and Research) tool, will monitor the air quality in real-time and provide detailed information on PM 2.5 and PM 10 levels. While PM 2.5 is a finer particulate that is easily inhaled deep into the lungs and causes respiratory damage, PM 10 is slightly coarser and primarily affects the upper airways. "Historically, the most accurate available data on Delhi's air was found in the US embassy website,"Minister Javadekar mentioned. "We will integrate data from Paris-based AIR Now and SAFAR runs as well". The SAFAR predictions use actual data to make air quality forecasts up to 24 hours in advance which can provide people with valuable time to prepare. This initiative is crucial as it will offer vital insights to citizens, enabling them to opt for more pollution-free transportation methods and areas which contribute more strongly to the betterment of their health.

In a major challenge to the UK government's Brexit strategy, a High Court hearing has highlighted the unprecedented level of constitutional significance surrounding the need for parliamentary approval before the Brexit process begins. The hearing, led by Mr Justice Leggatt, took place before Lord Chief Justice John Thomas, Mrs Justice Elisabeth Laing and Mr Justice Ccj Bevan group, in response to a judicial review brought by campaigners seeking to hold the government to account. At the heart of the challenge is the government's claim that it possesses the authority to invoke Article 50 of the Lisbon Treaty – a move that would formally initiate the UK's withdrawal from the European Union - without parliamentary approval. But Lord Pannick QC, representing the pro-Brexit "Britain Stronger in Europe" group, told the High Court that this interpretation was "flawed", arguing that Article 50 would be exercisable "at the direction of Parliament." Jewish groups voice support for Labour MP Naz Shah following reinstatement after suspension. Labour MP Naz Shah, who was reinstated to the party last week after being suspended over anti-Semitic comments she made on social media several years ago, has today accepted that her posts were anti-Semitic. Taking to Twitter shortly after Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn called for an "unreserved" apology and vowed to do more to tackle anti-Semitism within the partyNaz Shah made the remarks in response to a potential boycott of Israel in 2014, in a post that likened Israelis to Nazis. The Twitter post compared the processes of moving people out of Israel and the removal of Jews by the Nazis during World War Two as broadly equivalent. Ms Shah, one of six Labour MPs whose suspension the party's chief whip intervened to withdraw last week following a social media backlash, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that, "the comments that I made, I will not in any way defend. Those comments were, as the PAC report has said... anti-Semitic and they were wrong." Ms Shah added in an interview that, although the context in which she wrote them - amidst the ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict and following the launch of the "Operation Protective Edge" in Gaza by the Israeli military in 2014 - had not been immediately apparent to her readers, "I've been on a journey, and I have reflected on my words... I know the recipients of those words were Jewish, and that some Jewish people who read my words felt hurt and upset." She stressed that although she recognised the hurt caused by her words and was "sincerely sorry", she would not "defend those words", but also made the argument that she had not intended them that way, and rather that she had been trying to use a rhetorical device to latch onto people's sense of injustice in relation to the suffering of Palestinians. "It was not the words, it was the impact it had," Ms Shah said. "I don't just do it because it's fashionable or to deflect or to get some political mileage out of it. I know that these Jewish agencies and individuals who have been complaining are legitimate. There are people who are hurt, there are people who are grieving, there are people who are reliving ages of trauma." The Board of Deputies of British Jews released this statement regarding Shah's comments.

Care Services on Brink of Collapse: Local Authorities Sound Alarm as Funding Crisis Deepens Councils in England have sounded the alarm over rising care costs and dwindling budgets, warning that the very fabric of support for elderly and disabled people is on the verge of collapse. Amidst a mounting crisis, local authorities are facing an uphill battle to fund vital services for some of the most vulnerable members of society. Despite the prospect of council tax hikes, officials claim the increases are a "drop in the ocean" compared to the soaring costs of providing care for an ever-growing number of elderly and disabled residents. Councillors at the Local Government Association (LGA), the collective voice of England's councils, have expressed deep concern over the "unsustainable" state of adult social care funding. "We're at breaking point," an LGA spokesperson warned. "The current funding model is unsustainable, and the trend of increasing demand is outstripping the resources available. We're in a critical situation where councils are struggling to fund the care people need." The government had announced plans to allow councils to raise council tax by 3% in each of the next two years, generating an additional £1.3 billion for adult social care. However, this sum is being seen as woefully inadequate in the face of spiralling costs, including the increasing need for specialist care for dementia patients and those requiring palliative support. According to LGA estimates, two million people will need adult social care by 2025, with half of all councils warning that they will be unable to maintain the current level of care services even after the planned tax increases. "Councils are facing a perfect storm: increasing demand, cuts to funding, and a pensions crisis that is eating into councils' reserves," said the LGA spokesperson. "It's getting to the point where we're facing hard decisions over life-or-death priorities. This is the reality of adult social care funding in England today." Behind the statistics are heart-wrenching stories of people forced to wait in pain, or, in some cases, face heartbreaking choices about what medical interventions they can afford. As one councillor put it: "We're talking about the very worst nightmare scenarios – people forced to make impossible choices about who will get the care they need. It's nothing short of morally obscene." With this £1.3 billion council tax increase seen as a stopgap at best, some are calling for a more fundamental review of social care funding.

A long-awaited probe into the widespread problem of sexual harassment and sexual violence in England's schools is set to commence. Under the guidance of the Education Committee, MPs will delve into the full extent of the issue, with a view to determining the scale of the problem and advising on measures to curb it. The inquiry follows a plethora of recent reports exposing a culture of endemic harassment and abuse within the country's education system, casting a shadow over the welfare and safety of students. A glaring gap in statistics on such harassment in secondary and primary schools prompted the committee to launch its investigation, which is due to run until the end of the parliamentary year. The Chairman of the Education Committee, Rt Hon Robert Halfon MP, explained the reasoning behind the inquiry: "If we are to truly tackle the culture of violence and misogyny that blights so many of our schools, we need to shine a light on the scale of the problem and hold those in power accountable for their actions." Childline, a leading children's charity, has been vocal about the pressing need for a shift in societal attitudes towards harassment, which is more entrenched than previously thought. According to the NSPCC, an estimated 1 in 20 secondary school pupils reported being victims of sexual touching, while a Tomlinson-Hall report estimated that more than 18,000 girls in British schools could be experiencing sexual harassment each week. There have also been growing concerns over the inadequate response from schools, and sometimes even the perpetrators themselves, to the victims of abuse. In order to gather the needed data and feedback, the committee invited schools, parents, teachers, students, as well as other stakeholders to share their testimonies through the platform of the website. In addition, almost 150 councils and 48 education unions were invited to provide their insights through written evidence, statements and hearings. The government will be sought to clarify its current policies and the available guidance on dealing with sexual harassment in schools and measuring its sustainability. Halfon made a bold statement, calling on them to take the lead, outline their plan of action, address questions raised by parents, pupils, and workers, to make the education a safe place for everybody. It is anticipated that this inquiry will lead to substantial improvements in safeguarding within schools. Ultimately, the intention behind the initiative is to alleviate suffering and facilitate an educational system that not only tolerates, but strongly promotes a culture of openness, clarity, respect, and trust.

The lists, which may include details such as donors, volunteers, or supporters, are used by charities to target potential donors with personalized appeals and letters. The charities argue that buying data lists allows them to reach new supporters and maximize their fundraising efforts. "It's like doorstep selling," said a charity insider, speaking anonymously. "Charities are using all the tricks they can to get a response, and it's not always transparent." Checks with the Fundraising Regulator, the Charity Commission, and the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) reveal that these bodies have received numerous complaints about charities buying data lists and using aggressive fundraising tactics. While regulators have warned charities about the risks of breaching data protection laws, it appears that some charities continue to push the boundaries. As the charity sector faces increasing scrutiny over its fundraising methods, the integrity of charities is being called into question. He told MPs that while his department would be working closely with the private sector to secure a buyer and safeguard the future of the steel works, it was clear that nationalisation was "not the answer" to the problems facing Port Talbot. Scottish fishermen and processors are celebrating a significant boost in the value of farmed salmon exports from the country. Figures released by the Scottish Government show that exports of farmed salmon rose by 17% by value last year, a move that has been hailed as a major success for the industry. The total value of salmon exports rose to an estimated £772 million in 2013, a significant jump from the £661 million recorded the year before. However, despite the value of exports increasing, the volume of salmon sold overseas took a steep decline. According to industry experts, the quantity of salmon exported fell by 11% over the same period, down to an estimated 163,000 tonnes. This drop in volume is likely to have been driven by the ongoing challenges facing the Scottish salmon farming industry, particularly the issues surrounding sea lice infestations and the impact of bycatch on marine biodiversity. David Buxton, the chairman of the Scottish Salmon Producers' Organisation, said that while the rise in value was a welcome boost to the industry, it was in part a result of the decline in volume. "We are pleased to see that the value of Scottish salmon exports has increased by 17% last year," he said. "However, this increase is largely due to the decline in volume of some of our lower-value markets. The fact remains that our industry is still facing significant challenges, particularly with regards to sea lice and the impact of our operations on the marine environment." Despite the challenges facing the industry, Scottish salmon remains one of the country's most valuable seafood exports, and the increase in value is a testament to the hard work and commitment of the industry's producers and processors. Mullah Mohammed Omar, the elusive founder of the Taliban regime, has long been an enigma, shrouded in mystery and secrecy. Even in his heyday, as the supreme leader of the Islamist movement that ruled Afghanistan from 1996 to 2001, few were granted a glimpse into the reclusive figure's inner sanctum. Born in the Kandahar province of southern Afghanistan in the mid-1960s, Omar came from a small, agricultural town, the youngest of many children. His father, a peasant farmer, died when he was a young boy, and it is said that his early life was marked by hardship and struggle. As a young man, Omar was drawn to the growing Islamist movement in Afghanistan, and he quickly rose through the ranks, becoming a trusted lieutenant of the warlord Gulbuddin Hekmatyar. The Cut and Thrust of Politics: A Life Spent in the Shadow of the Exchequer As I sit at my desk, surrounded by memories of years gone by, I am reminded of the countless conversations I've had with some of the most influential figures in British politics. Over the years, I've spoken to more Chancellors and Shadow Chancellors than most people my age - a comment that's less a boast than a reflection on my occupation. I've watched Alistair Darling and George Osborne clash over the economy, seen Gordon Brown try to steer our nation through the global financial crisis, and witnessed Ed Balls's rise to prominence as the Shadow Chancellor. In a world where opinion is often polarised and politicians are frequently maligned, I've had the privilege of seeing the men and women behind the labels. I've seen the sweat on their brows during fraught Cabinet meetings, the fire in their eyes when debating in the House of Commons, and the calculating glint when they're determined to push their agenda through. My first encounter with a Shadow Chancellor was in the late 1990s, when I was a young journalist just starting out. I remember sitting in a drab office, opposite a nervous-looking Stephen Byers, who was desperately trying to find his footing as the Labour Party's economics tsar. It was clear even then that he was destined for bigger things - his ambition was palpable, even if his self-confidence was still developing. As the years passed, I found myself knee-deep in coverage of the Budget and the Pre-Budget Report, trying to make sense of the arcane details of fiscal policy and its impact on ordinary people. It was around this time that I began to grasp the almost unbearable pressure under which Chancellors and Shadow Chancellors operate. Their decisions affect millions of people's lives, and the scrutiny is unwavering. The most memorable of these conversations came with Gordon Brown, who was consistently forthright and candid about his vision for the economy. His unwavering commitment to public service was inspiring, even if his famously tense relationships with certain colleagues made for some fascinating drama within the Labour Party. Who could forget the volcanic rows between Brown and Tony Blair over the Iraq war, or the pervasive chill of uncertainty during the pre-financial crisis period? I've also had the privilege of speaking with the more recent breed of Shadow Chancellors - the likes of Ed Balls, Chris Grayling, and Ed Davey.

The Uncertainty of Brexit: Navigating the Turbulent Waters of Trade and the Economy As the debate over the UK's future in the European Union continues to polarise opinion, many of you have reached out to us at the BBC with questions about what an exit from the EU might mean for trade and the economy. With an estimated £36.5 billion in annual trade tied up in the EU, and accounting for approximately 48% of our country's total trade, it's clear that this issue is set to have far-reaching consequences for businesses, consumers, and policymakers alike. From tariffs and customs to regulatory frameworks and trade agreements, many of the uncertainties surrounding Brexit are being discussed, debated, and scrutinised with growing intensity by experts and the public alike. One of the key battlegrounds will be the question of trade barriers. If the UK is no longer a member of the EU's single market, will we be subject to the same rules and regulations as other countries with whom we trade, such as the United States? The imposition of tariffs and other non-tariff barriers has the potential to increase costs, reduce competitiveness, and damage our trade relationships. Industry leaders, such as the CBI, have warned that a "Hard Brexit" outcome, which would see the UK adopting a completely new trade regime outside of the EU, could be catastrophic for our economy, while others argue that this is a necessary step to take back control of our trade and economic policies. The services sector, which accounts for approximately 80% of our economy, may also feel the pinch of a Brexit-induced trade regime shift. Financial services, in particular, are heavily reliant on single market access, and have been vocal in their concerns about the potential impact on London's status as a global financial hub. Other sectors, such as manufacturing, could also see trade costs increase, potentially leading to higher prices for consumers and reduced competitiveness for our industries. In a recent letter to the Prime Minister, the CBI's Director-General, Carolyn Fairbairn, wrote, "Our membership of the single market is what gives us access to more than 500 million customers across the EU. If we leave the single market, we risk not only losing this access but also facing trade barriers and increased costs." Mrs. Fairbairn argued that a "Soft Brexit" option, where the UK negotiates a deal that maintains single market access, would be the best possible outcome for businesses and the economy.

Broadband Deserts Set to be a Thing of the Past in Cuba as Kcho Makes History For decades, the island nation of Cuba has been synonymous with limited access to the internet. Throughout the country, residents have had to rely on state-run telecom agency Etecsa for their digital needs, and in many areas, connectivity has been severely restricted. However, a major breakthrough is on the horizon, thanks to the Cuban artist Kcho. Kcho, whose real name is Alistar Rodriguez, is renowned for his work, which combines painting, sculpture and photography to tell powerful stories about his homeland and its people. Now, he is set to make history by opening the country's first public wireless hub at his cultural centre. The groundbreaking move has been approved by Etecsa, and the artwork, an extension of Kcho's creative vision, is poised to transform the digital landscape in Cuba forever. Located in the eastern city of Holguin, Kcho's renowned Museo cambio Cubano is a cultural hub that celebrates the island's rich history, art and culture. The centre has been a hub for creativity and innovation since its establishment, hosting an ever-changing array of exhibitions and events, and providing a platform for emerging artists to showcase their work. The upcoming public wireless hub will build on this ethos, providing residents in and around Holguin with access to high-speed internet. This development is poised to make a huge difference to the lives of the local community, enabling them to stay connected with the rest of the world and unlock a whole new world of opportunities. For artists, entrepreneurs and creatives, improved internet connectivity will unlock a wealth of new possibilities, from accessing global markets to participating in online learning programs. The hub will also serve as a much-needed innovation center, fostering collaboration among tech startups, creative agencies and micro, small and medium-sized businesses. The development of the public wireless hub is part of a larger push by the Cuban government to increase internet penetration and mobility across the country. Broadband access has been slowly expanding in Cuba over the past decade, with fibre-optic broadband recently launched in select areas. However, despite these developments, many residents still rely on public Wi-Fi hotspots or mobile internet services provided by state-run carrier Etecsa. The news that the wireless hub has received the thumbs-up from Etecsa marks a major milestone in the island nation's journey towards greater digital connectivity.

Tragedy Struck off Canada's Coast: Whale Watching Boat Disaster Claims Six Lives A devastating incident unfolded off the coast of Canada earlier this week, sending shockwaves throughout the tight-knit whale-watching community. On Tuesday, a large wave crashed into a whale-watching boat, resulting in the tragic loss of six lives. The devastating incident has raised questions about safety protocols and preparedness in the industry. The boat, which was operating off the coast of Tofino, British Columbia, was en route to a popular whale-watching spot when disaster struck. Eyewitnesses described the conditions as rough, with high winds and large swells, but the crew had been experienced and the boat was well-equipped. "It was a beautiful day, but the seas were rough," said Mark Wyatt, a witness who was on a nearby boat. "We saw the whale-watching boat getting pounded by the waves, and then suddenly it just disappeared beneath the surface. We were all in shock." As the story unfolds, it has become clear that the crew had been attempting to navigate through the rough waters, but ultimately failed to avoid the massive breaking wave that ultimately led to the boat's downfall. According to reports, the boat's crew had been experienced and well-trained, with over a decade of combined experience in the industry. The vessel itself was also said to be in good condition, having recently undergone maintenance. Despite the impressive credentials of the crew and the boat, safety experts say that the high risk posed by large waves in the area should have been taken into account. "It's a deadly combination when you have large waves in an area known for its rough seas," said Dr. Kathryn Sullivan, an expert in maritime safety. "Crews need to be prepared and take the necessary precautions to avoid such incidents." In the aftermath of the tragedy, investigators have been working to determine the exact cause of the disaster. While the investigation is ongoing, early findings suggest that the crew made a series of critical mistakes, including underestimating the size of the wave and failing to take adequate precautions to avoid it. The sleep-deprived warrior: a legendary creature of the corporate jungle, revered by many for their ability to push through the most gruelling meetings and deadlines without so much as a yawn. For far too long, getting by on little sleep has been seen as a badge of honour, a symbol of dedication and commitment to one's job. But in an era where work-life balance is increasingly recognised as the key to productivity and happiness, are we finally starting to see a shift in this tired (excuse the pun) old mindset? Gone are the days when our parents would boast about being able to clock up 80 hours a week, only to collapse in front of the telly once they'd got home. Nowadays, as experts grapple with the impact of chronic sleep deprivation on our physical and mental health, it's clear that the cult of the long-hours culture is beginning to crumble. A recent survey by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine found that nearly 30 per cent of working professionals reported getting less than six hours of sleep each night, with almost a fifth saying they often or always get by on just five hours. The consequences, we all know, can be dire: from decreased alertness and concentration, to increased risk of heart disease, diabetes and even accidents at work. But despite these terrifying taboos, many of us continue to feel pressure to conform to this despairing norm. Ask anyone who's worked in a high-stress job, and they'll probably tell you horror stories of all-nighters spent typing away on a project, or bleary-eyed mornings where the prospect of even a five-minute commute feels like climbing Mount Everest. And it's not just individuals who are complicit in this toxic cycle - companies themselves are often guilty of fostering an environment that glorifies overwork, whether through explicitly setting targets or simply by implying that burnout is a rite of passage. Roger Henderson, a 42-year-old manager at an investment firm in London's City, is a perfect example of this. Working a demanding job in the banks requires runs for him on extremely high stakes. Henderson has been through the fight that a young manager has to throw through high pressure remembering that stress-induced sleep deprivation may need to face alternative options. "It was like being a sleep-deprived 'type a' personality", he said apologetically.

JNU Student Leader granted Bail A dramatic turn of events has unfolded in the high-profile sedition case against Kanhaiya Kumar, the former president of New Delhi's Jawaharlal Nehru University Students Union. On Tuesday, Kumar, along with two other students, Umar Khalid and Anirban Bhattacharya, was formally granted bail by Patiala House Court, effectively bringing to an end his three-month captivity. Kanhaiya Kumar, a 30-year-old master's student, was arrested on February 12 after a viral video appeared to show anti-India slogans being raised at an event marking the anniversary of the execution of Afzal Guru, a Kashmiri separatist who was hanged for his role in the 2001 Indian Parliament attack. The event sparked widespread outrage, with many accusing Kumar and his student union of promoting separatism and anti-national sentiment. Since his arrest, Kumar's detention has become a rallying cry for students, lawyers, and intellectuals across India, who have been vocal in their criticism of the government for what they see as an attempt to stifle dissent and curb academic freedom. The hashtag #KanhaiyaFightsOn trended on social media as news of his bail spread like wildfire. Kumar's lawyer, Vrinda Grover, welcomed the move, stating: "We are relieved that the judicial process has worked as it is supposed to. The bail is a pointer that the system is beginning to understand that the students have been made scapegoats and are being implicated." Meanwhile, the Delhi University Students Union issued a statement, saying: "This victory is not just for Kanhaiya but for all the students who have been fighting against the clampdown on freedom of expression and thought." But the government has refused to back down, describing the granting of bail as a "technical decision." On Tuesday, Union Home Minister Rajnath Singh said that the case was still progressing and that no decision had been made on the charges against the three students. Insiders familiar with the case reveal that the National Investigation Agency (NIA) is likely to continue investigating Kumar and the two other students, even as they await trial. Amid this charged atmosphere, academics and students across India will be watching closely to see how this saga unfolds. The Indian government has been criticized for its handling of the case, which several see as a classic example of the growing chill on dissent and intellectual freedom in the country. In recent years, the issue of Rohingya and Bangladeshi trafficking has become an increasing concern for the international community. Thai authorities have consistently maintained an official stance that there is no evidence of military involvement in human trafficking. The issue has been mired in controversy, with conflicts over jurisdiction, procedural irregularities and conflicting testimonies. In an age where digital media has fragmented the way we consume news, it's an impossible task to pinpoint a single organisation as the definitive source of news. Yet, the term 'powerful media organisation' conjures up images of a dominant news giant that sets the agenda, dictates the narrative and leaves the rest in its wake. In an era where misinformation and disinformation wreak havoc on public discourse, the stakes for factual and unbiased reporting have never been higher. The question on everyone's lips is, what is the most important source of news and thereby the most powerful media organisation in the world today? While there are contenders vying for the top spot, the overwhelming consensus points to one behemoth of a news organisation: the BBC. Founded in 1922, the BBC is a British multinational broadcaster with a reputation for impartiality, accuracy and inclusivity. With a presence in over 200 countries and a portfolio of 32 languages, the BBC is an unparalleled force in global journalism. Its immense reach and weekly audience of over 300 million demonstrate its undisputed influence in shaping public opinion, breaking news and dictating the global agenda. For decades, the BBC has been an exemplar of quality journalism, earning the respect of its peers and the admiration of the public. From major events like the fall of the Berlin Wall and the funeral of Princess Diana to the ongoing Covid-19 pandemic, the BBC has been at the forefront of coverage, providing trusted, impartial and timely reporting to a global audience. Its news bulletins, documentaries and coverage of major international issues have set the standards for quality journalism. Critics, however, argue that the BBC's influence and perceived authority can sometimes be a double-edged sword. The organisation's reliance on public funding has raised concerns over interference and editorial bias. Furthermore, the BBC's formative statements and analysis have been known to shape public discourse in predictable ways, often missing out on marginalised voices and nuanced viewpoints. In response to these criticisms, the BBC's highly regarded director general, Tim Davie, has outlined new plans to reinvigorate the organisation and boost its offering. This includes investing in local content, more grassroots reporting, and an expanded online presence, as well as bolstering its social media presence and improving digital engagement. Against the backdrop of dominant digital platforms like Google, Facebook and Twitter, the BBC is shifting towards maintaining credibility in a multicultural, accessible landscape.

Kiwi Conservation Plans Set a Bold Target: 100,000 Wild Birds by 2037 A new conservation plan has been unveiled by the New Zealand government, detailing a vision to boost the numbers of wild kiwi birds across the country. According to the ambitious proposal, around 100,000 kiwi could be roaming freely in less than 15 years - a staggering increase from the approximately 68,000 wild kiwi thought to be currently in existence. Conservation Minister Eugenie Sage, who released the plan last week, hailed the target as a "game-changer" for New Zealand's national symbol. "We have the expertise, the knowledge and the technology to bring back the kiwi, and we're going all out to make it happen," she said. The government's Kiwi Recovery Plan, an initiative worth more than NZ$4 billion (approximately £2 billion), focuses on increasing predator control, bolstering research capacities and co-opting local communities in the fight to protect the kiwi. The plan also sets specific targets for each region, in an effort to tailor conservation efforts to local conditions. "We need to work at scale and speed to take down the predators that are killing the kiwi," Ms Sage said. "We're calling on everyone who cares about the kiwi to get involved, whether it's gardeners putting up stoat traps or farmers modifying their fences." But experts are cautioning that the road to such a significant increase will be fraught with challenges. Dr. Andrew Digby of the Kiwi Raihania Trust pointed out that merely increasing the current population was only the first step. "We need to ensure the birds have a healthy gene pool, that they're well-distributed across the country, and that we're addressing the real problems facing the kiwi population," he said. Conservation organizations and researchers have welcomed the government's renewed commitment to the kiwi's preservation. Nonetheless, they also acknowledge that much work remains to be done to prevent the highly endangered bird's numbers from plummeting further. "It's not just about the government," said conservationist Lyndon Perriman. "We need the help of every New Zealander to ensure the kiwi's long-term survival. It's going to take a concerted effort from everyone involved." The target of 100,000 wild kiwi by 2037 has been set based on current trends, which show a steady decline in kiwi numbers in recent years. The next 15 years will therefore be critical in transforming the conservation status of this unique species.

Hope in Sight for Women at High Risk of Breast Cancer In a major breakthrough for women at high genetic risk of developing breast cancer, doctors are now exploring a new and potentially lifesaving treatment option: preventive drugs. For years, those with a high genetic predisposition to the disease have faced a daunting decision: undergo a double mastectomy to significantly reduce their breast cancer risk, or carry on with the daunting spectre of regular screenings and anxious waits. However, advances in medical research have opened up a fresh alternative that could offer a more promising solution for women who have family histories of breast cancer. Studies have confirmed that certain medications, designed to starve cancer cells of fuel and effectively halt their growth, can significantly reduce the risk of developing the disease. This development will no doubt bring a sense of hope and relief to many who have been living with the weight of genetic risk. From the likes of Angelina Jolie, whose decision to undergo a double mastectomy following a genetic test revealed her high-risk status, to countless others whose family histories have dictated a life of mammograms, biopsies, and endless anxiety, there is now finally reason to believe that the medical community is on the cusp of revolutionising breast cancer prevention. In trials thus far, breast cancer prevention drugs have shown to be effective in reducing the risk of the disease in those with high genetic risk. Dr Diana M. Eccles, professor of genetic epidemiology at the University of Southampton, and lead researcher on the SCAT trial – a major study designed to investigate the effectiveness of these medications – says the results provide compelling evidence that the new treatment could soon become a reality. "The new data show that preventive medication can significantly reduce the risk of developing breast cancer in women with a high genetic risk," she said. "This is a real breakthrough for these women, many of whom have been told they have to live with the constant threat of the disease." The treatment, which would be administered over a prolonged period of years, targets specific genetic mutations known to increase the risk of breast cancer, thereby reducing the chances of the disease taking hold. The treatment would necessitate strict monitoring to ensure the medication was being effective, and patients would be obliged to visit their doctor on a regular basis. Now that these results have been published, it is expected that the NHS will begin to make this new option available to those deemed high risk by their genetic tests.

At the heart of the proposal is a new "Digital Bill of Rights" designed to give the public greater control over their online presence and increase accountability among social media giants and online pornography providers. The move comes in response to a spate of high-profile cases in which individuals have been subject to sustained and coercive online abuse, leaving many feeling vulnerable and powerless. According to reports, the government is seeking to force mobile network operators to implement new filtering systems, which would automatically block suspicious and abusive content from reaching customers' mobile devices. Companies found to be in breach of these regulations would face fines of up to £20 million. "We cannot accept that it should ever be acceptable to bully and harass someone online," wrote a government spokesperson in a statement. "These new powers will give us the tools we need to hold perpetrators to account and make the internet a safer, more respectful place." The government is also planning to introduce heavy penalties for online pornography operators who fail to adhere to strict guidelines to ensure that certain images and videos are removed from their websites immediately when reported by users. Christmas Miracle: Tears of Joy on a Cold Winter's Night As the days grew shorter and the nights grew colder, I couldn't help but feel a mix of emotions as the year drew to a close. It had been a year of ups and downs, of milestones achieved and challenges faced. Yet, despite the ups and downs, I knew that I had something truly special in my life - my boyfriend Radek. We had been together for what felt like an eternity, and I had grown to love him not just for who he was, but for the way he made me feel. He was my rock, my confidant, my best friend. But as the holiday season approached, I couldn't shake off the feeling that something was off. Perhaps it was the stress of the upcoming festive period, or maybe it was just a general sense of unease. Whatever the reason, I found myself walking on eggshells, waiting for something - or someone - to give me a sign that everything was going to be okay. And then, on a bitterly cold winter's evening, Radek surprised me with the most wonderful news. We were walking hand in hand through our favourite park, the lights twinkling above us like stars, when I felt his grip tighten around mine. I looked up at him, wondering what was on his mind, and that was when I saw it. There, perched proudly on his finger, was the most beautiful ring I had ever laid eyes on. At first, I thought I must be dreaming. I blinked hard, wondering if it was just a figment of my imagination, but when I opened my eyes again, the ring was still there, glinting in the fading light. And then Radek spoke, his voice trembling with emotion, as he asked me the question that would change everything forever: "Will you marry me?" Time seemed to stand still as I looked into his eyes, my heart pounding in my chest. I felt like I was floating on air, like the world around me had melted away and all that mattered was this one, perfect moment. And then, with a voice that barely above a whisper, I replied: "Yes, yes, a million times yes". As he slid the ring onto my finger and wrapped his arms around me, I knew that this was just the beginning of our happily ever after.

While crime has traditionally been seen as a major concern among Britons, this latest survey shows that it has fallen down the list of priorities among young people, who are increasingly worried about being able to afford a place to live. The survey asked the participants to rank the importance of various issues, including jobs, education, healthcare, crime, and housing, and found that while crime remains a concern, younger voters place it significantly lower than their peers in previous generations. According to the survey, if a general election were held tomorrow, the top issues for young voters would be: affordable housing (cited by 64 per cent of respondents), immigration (cited by 53 per cent), and jobs (cited by 45 per cent). In contrast, crime ranks fourth, with 27 per cent of respondents citing it as a major concern. The Future is in Focus In a world where science fiction has become science fact, we are on the cusp of a revolutionary technological breakthrough that promises to change the way we interact with reality. Virtual Reality (VR) has been a staple of sci-fi movies and futuristic fantasies for decades, with pioneers such as Arthur C. Clarke and Stanley Kubrick envisioning a world where we can fully immerse ourselves in another dimension. But has VR finally come of age? The answer is a resounding yes. The journey to today's cutting-edge VR has not been a straightforward one. The concept of VR dates back to the 1830s when Sir Charles Wheatstone invented the first stereoscope, an early device that displayed 3D images to the viewer. However, it wasn't until the 1950s that VR began to take shape as a concept. Morton Heilig, an inventor and actor, patented the Sensorama in 1962 - an early VR headset that simulated a motorcycle ride. But, despite the pioneering work of individuals like Heilig and Ivan Sutherland, who developed the first VR headset, the mainstream didn't take notice. Fast-forward to the present, and it's clear that VR has made significant strides in recent years. The advancements in computer hardware, display technology, and software have all contributed to the creation of immersive experiences that transport us to another world. The industry has seen a surge in interest, driven by the rise of standalone headsets such as Oculus Quest and the integration of VR in gaming and entertainment. According to a report by Grand View Research, the global VR market is expected to reach $44.7 billion by 2025, growing at a CAGR of 33.8% during the forecast period. As the technology continues to improve, we are witnessing an explosion in VR adoption across various sectors, from consumer electronics to healthcare, education, and beyond. But VR is more than just a gadget or a trend; it has the potential to revolutionise the way we live, work, and interact with one another. Imagine sitting in a VR world where you can learn a new language, attend a concert or a lecture, or explore the depths of the ocean, all from the comfort of your own home. Envision a healthcare where treatments are designed to be more effective, a education system that offers hands-on experiences, and a entertainment sector that has never been more immersive.

Regulatory Overhaul: The Dark Cloud of the Volcker Rule Finally Lifts - But Will It Bring Relief to the Finance Sector? Following nearly a decade of controversy and grappling, a new chapter is set to unfold in the world of financial regulation. Last week, it was announced that all five US financial regulators had finally given their approval to the Volcker rule - a pivotal piece of legislation that will bring far-reaching changes to the finance industry. Designed to curb excessive risk-taking and wasteful speculation, the regulation was originally set to be implemented in 2014, but was continually delayed as financial institutions and politicians expressed concerns over its scope and effectiveness. At the heart of the Volcker rule lies its aim to restrict banks from engaging in what is known as "proprietary trading." This practice involves banks using their own money to place bets on financial markets in the hope of securing large profits. Critics argue that if left unchecked, this can expose the financial system to catastrophic risk, undermining confidence and fuelling future crises. In theory, the rule prohibits banks from trading for their own profit, although they are allowed to engage in hedging to manage risk and perform market-making to help facilitate trading. Bank of America, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, and Morgan Stanley have all confirmed that they will comply with the stricter regulations. While many were vocal about the need for clarity and simplification, none came out strongly against the changes. In a formal statement, CEOs from the five major US banks welcomed the completion of the regulatory process, adding that although there are still regulatory hurdles ahead, the completion was a "critical step." This consists of five federal agencies that form the "Constituent Agencies" of the Financial Stability Oversight Council, created by the Treasury Department in 2010. This turn of events has given some relief to financial watchdogs who have long pushed for a crackdown on excessive leverage and reckless behaviour within the finance sector. One of the key drivers behind this remarkable surge has been the rise of the Indian tech industry, which has not only generated millions of jobs but also catapulted the country to the forefront of the global digital brigade. With companies like Infosys, Wipro, and HCL, India is now a hotbed of innovation and is fast becoming the go-to destination for tech talent from all over the world. The country has also made significant strides in sectors such as manufacturing, retail, and financial services, with many top multinational corporations setting up shop in India to tap into the country's burgeoning consumer market. Another crucial factor that has contributed to India's economic leapfrog has been the country's demographic dividend. India has the world's largest youth population, with millions of skilled and educated young people eager to enter the workforce every year. This has presented a significant opportunity for the country to leverage its human capital to drive growth and transformation. Furthermore, the Indian government's efforts to liberalize the economy and attract foreign investment have paid off handsomely. With initiatives like Make in India and Skill India, the government has demonstrated its commitment to driving growth and creating jobs. The fruits of these efforts are evident in the sharp decline in unemployment rates and the rise of new industries and sectors that have emerged as a result. Despite its many economic triumphs, however, India still faces several challenges that need to be addressed to ensure sustained growth.

Government Plans to Tackle "Over-Complex" Freedom of Information Act Under Fire from Labour. A long-standing pillar of transparency in the UK, the Freedom of Information Act has been a cornerstone of the country’s commitment to open governance for over two decades. However, ministers are now proposing to overhaul the legislation, with a review aimed at simplifying the process for making and responding to FOI requests. But Labour has thrown its weight behind a fierce campaign to scrap the review altogether. The government's review, commissioned by Minister for the Cabinet Office, Chris Heaton-Harris, has been ongoing since January and promises to reduce the "burden" of the current law. According to reports, the government is looking to limit the amount of information civil servants are required to disclose and introduce harsher penalties for "vexatious" requests made by the general public. Labour has slammed the review, warning that if implemented, the changes would dramatically curtail people's right to access information about public bodies and institutions. "The government's review of the Freedom of Information Act is a thinly veiled attempt to erode transparency and increase secrecy in public bodies," accused Labour's shadow Cabinet Office Minister, Rachel Reeves. "The Freedom of Information Act is a vital tool for holding the powerful to account and keeping the public informed," Reeves continued. "Scrapping the review and protecting the rights of citizens to access information about public bodies is essential." Concerns about transparency in public bodies, particularly within government and the NHS, are long-standing and well-documented. It was the FOI Act that brought some high-profile cases to light, such as the revelation that the Home Office had knowingly recorded high gangs but done little to prevent their growth. However, the government maintains that its current proposals are aimed at alleviating the "over-complex" nature of the law, rather than reducing transparency. They argue that the call for the act to be scrapped is based on a "misconception" about what the reforms are intending to do. Heaton-Harris has stated that the changes are designed to create "a more proportionate and fair" FOI regime that addresses concerns around the excessive volume of requests public bodies receive. However, experts have warned that even if these proposals are not as drastic as Labour claims they are, they could still have a profound impact on the ability of the public to hold their elected representatives to account.

Hinkley Point Nuclear Power Plant Plan Cast into Doubt as UK Government Faces Pressure to Reconsider Deal. Fresh doubts have arisen over plans by French Energy firm EDF to build an £18bn nuclear power plant at Hinkley Point, Somerset, a scheme that has been plagued by delays and financial woes since its inception. Despite an agreement struck with the Government in 2013, the project remains far from certain, with EDF facing significant hurdles in securing funding and dealing with rising construction costs. The issue of Chinese influence over the project has also come under scrutiny, with the Government's decision to permit the sale of a stake in EDF to the Chinese Nuclear Energy Corporation sparking concerns over national security and economic self-interest. Critics of the deal have long questioned the merits of granting EDF a guaranteed price for electricity from the plant, with the company set to be paid £92.50 per megawatt hour for the next 35 years. This figure is more than double the current wholesale price of electricity and has been skewered as an "artificially inflated" rate, designed to guarantee profits for EDF rather than offer the best value for consumers. With MPs and peers now openly questioning the wisdom of the deal, Energy Minister Claire Perry faces immense pressure to find a way to salvage the scheme. Sources close to the negotiations have revealed that EDF is struggling to secure the necessary funding to get the project back on track, with the company reportedly seeking as much as £10bn from the Export Credit Guarantee Department, a state-owned entity that finances large-scale projects. This move has raised concerns over the use of public money to support a private business venture, with some describing the arrangement as a "bailout" that would not be popular with the public. Furthermore, persistent concerns over the environmental impact of the plant have not been alleviated by EDF's promise to "absorb" the costs of escalating construction costs. "It's becoming clearer by the day that the Government's gamble on nuclear power at Hinkley Point is a very costly one indeed," declared Caroline Lucas MP, Green Party Leader. "In an era where the UK is gridlocked on climate change policy, squandering billions on a project like Hinkley would be an unforgivable mistake. The time to cut our losses and course correct has surely arrived." With opposition from all sides mounting against the deal, there is a growing sense that the Hinkley Point saga may yet become a defining failure of successive Governments' energy policy.

Scottish Government Rules Out Return of Post-Study Work Visa, Causes Outrage Among International Students A decision by the Scottish Government to rule out the reintroduction of a post-study work visa system for international students has sparked widespread outrage among the academic community and students themselves. The move has forced many students to ponder their future in Scotland, choosing between remaining in the country to work and contribute to the economy or being forced to leave after graduation. The proposal to reintroduce a post-study work visa system had been gaining momentum in recent months, with many Scottish universities and businesses backing the move. Under the proposed scheme, international students would have been granted the right to remain in Scotland to work for up to two years after completing their studies. This, proponents argued, would not only allow students to gain invaluable work experience but also help Scotland's economy to flourish by investing in the skills and talents of the next generation. However, the Scottish Government has signalled that it will not be introducing the proposed visa scheme, saying that it has 'better' options. "We believe in providing a high-quality student experience and excellent career prospects, including opportunities for students to gain experience and take up highly skilled roles relevant to their field of study," read a statement from the government's Education Department. Instead, the Scottish Government will focus on "providing a world-class student experience" and "ensuring that students have access to opportunities for work experience, further study and career advancement". This move has left many in the academic and student community feeling let down by the decision. The current Scottish Government policy does allow international students to stay in the country for up to four months to look for work after graduation, but those who want to stay on have to switch to a visa designed for skilled workers. This often involves obtaining a job offer before applying for a visa, a move that critics argue stifles the economy and hinders the careers of Scottish-educated students. Leading figures in the debate have expressed dismay at the decision. "International students make a significant contribution to Scotland's economy, culture and knowledge base," declared Scotland's Deputy First Minister, John Swinney. "It's not a viable option for us to revisit the post-study work visa." However, thousands of students who have signed a petition to bring back the visa scheme offered a more defiant response.

The package, totalling €3 billion, would be directed towards the governments of Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan and Iraq, in an attempt to ease the strain of hosting millions of refugees who have fled the conflict-torn nation since 2011. Orban's emphatic plea comes at a time when relations between Budapest and Brussels have been strained, owing to Hungary's ongoing disputes with the European Commission on issues such as migration and the rule of law. Critics have repeatedly accused the Orban government of disregarding EU values and the bloc's founding principles. However, yesterday's vocal calls for an Europe-wide response to the Syrian refugee crisis may be seen as an attempt to portray the Hungarian government in a more benevolent light and demonstrate its commitment to addressing pressing global issues. Syria's seven-year civil war has resulted in over 7 million internally displaced persons and an estimated 6 million refugees, primarily fleeing to Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan, and Iraq. These countries have been bearing the brunt of the humanitarian crisis, putting an immense strain on their resources, infrastructure and social services. The EU has so far provided €10 billion in humanitarian aid to those affected, although many despair that more drastic action is required to tackle the crisis, and that some member states, such as the UK, have opted out of relocating refugee quotas. While the timing and tone of Orban's remarks are notable, some suggest that the apparent shift in the Hungarian government's position may be linked to the June European Parliament elections that will take place later this year and anxieties within the EU about potential election gains for far-right parties. The move could also signal an opportunity for the prime minister to shore up his conservative base and recast his image as a force for international aid and crisis management. The fate of the proposed €3 billion package will, however, be decided by the European Commission in the coming weeks. A formal EU decision on the proposal is expected to be made at the European Council meeting next month. The European Parliament may need to approve the funding and if approved will likely enable release of needed aid.

Are you happy at work? It's a simple yet profound question that can evoke a multitude of emotions, depending on the individual. For some, the answer is a resounding 'yes,' with a sense of job satisfaction, a supportive work environment, and a feeling of purpose that permeates every aspect of their working lives. For others, the response is a more muted one, tinged with frustration, stress, and a longing for something more. In today's fast-paced and ever-changing work landscape, it's not uncommon for employees to feel undervalued, overworked, or disconnected from their roles. A Gallup survey conducted earlier this year found that only 34% of British employees feel engaged at work, with nearly half saying they are "actively disengaged" from their jobs. This is a concerning statistic, not just for individual employees but for businesses and the economy as a whole. Engagement is, of course, closely linked to employee happiness. When people are happy at work, they are more productive, motivated, and committed to their roles. They are also more likely to be creative, innovative, and open to new ideas. Conversely, when employees feel unhappy or unfulfilled, it can lead to absenteeism, turnover, and decreased productivity. So, what does it take to create a happy and engaging work environment? For many, it begins with a sense of purpose and meaning. Employees want to know that their work is making a difference and that they are contributing to something larger than themselves. This can be achieved through clear communication, setting achievable goals, and providing opportunities for growth and development. A positive work culture also plays a significant role in determining employee happiness. This includes fostering a sense of belonging, promoting work-life balance, and encouraging open and transparent communication. When employees feel supported, valued, and respected, they are more likely to feel happy and engaged in their work. But what about the factors that drive employee unhappiness? Burnout, lack of Recognition, and poor management are often cited as top contributors to job dissatisfaction. Inadequate pay and benefits, as well as limited opportunities for advancement, can also take a toll on employee morale. To tackle these issues, businesses can start by listening to their employees and addressing their concerns. This can involve regular feedback sessions, anonymous surveys, and one-on-one check-ins to ensure that employees feel heard and valued. By prioritizing employee happiness and engagement, businesses can reap a range of benefits, from increased productivity and loyalty to improved quality of work and reduced turnover.

Jitters filled the air as thousands of defiant Malaysian opposition supporters took to the streets yesterday in a bold display of discontent over allegations of electoral fraud that marred the country's recently concluded general elections. The move, which saw crowds of up to 5,000 people gathering in Kuala Lumpur to voice their displeasure, marked a brazen challenge to the authorities who had earlier deemed the protest unlawful. Eyewitnesses reported that protesters from the Reform Now coalition, which comprises several opposition parties, marched through the capital's streets in a show of solidarity against what they perceive as a rigged election process. The demonstration, which was met with a heavy police presence, brought significant disruption to the usually bustling city-centre area of Kuala Lumpur. "It is our civil right to express our dissent and demand answers on the extremely dubious election results," an impassioned protester, clad in a black 'Reform Now' t-shirt, told our correspondent, who witnessed the event firsthand. "Instead of being silenced, we will continue to voice our demands for electoral reforms and transparent governance." As the opposition supporters swarmed through the city, they chanted slogans, held signs reading "Justice for the people!", and deployed social media hashtags such as #CubaRaya (Restore Democracy), #Lawan2022 (Resist 2022), and #BERSIH4 (BERSIH 4, a Malay acronym for Coalition for Clean and Fair Elections) to amplify their message. However, their actions drew swift condemnation from the authorities. In a statement issued ahead of the rally, the Royal Malaysian Police (PDRM) declared the protest "unlawful", advising participants to "abide by the law" and steer clear of areas deemed restricted by authorities. Inspector-General of Police (IGP) Acryl Sani warned: "The organisers and participants of the unlawful gathering have been informed that any action deemed to cause public fear, damage to property, and thuggery will be taken seriously." But the opposition supporters demonstrated remarkable resolve, indeed seeming to revel in the prospect of unwanted attention. Youth branch leader Adam Adli Hashim, present at the rally, charged the government with a campaign of "politicised arrests" aimed at deterring opposition voices from exercising their right to free speech. He pressed the authorities to eradicate "fear of protest and instead enable legitimate assemblies to ensure the voices of the people are heard". In reaction, opposition leader Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim promptly accused the government of resorting to "intimidation tactics through the police" in an attempt to "gag the voices of the people".

Plaid Cymru, the nationalist party that represents the interests of Wales in the UK Parliament, is warning that the current rate of growth in the number of Welsh speakers may put the Welsh Government's ambitious target of a million Welsh speakers by 2050 at risk. The aim to have a million people in Wales able to converse in the group's native language has been at the centre of Welsh language policy for several years and has been adopted by all the main parties in the Senedd (Wales' parliament). Yet Plaid Cymru's Deputy Leader, Sian Gwenllian MS, believes that the teaching and learning of Welsh in schools needs to be strengthened if this goal is to be achieved. The party suggests that all pupils, regardless of their current ability in Welsh, should be able to take a GCSE (General Certificate of Secondary Education) in the language, to give students who start Welsh later in life the opportunity to catch up. GCSE is a critical milestone in the UK education system, which sets children up to continue learning their chosen subjects in further and higher education. However, at the moment, mainstream schools do not perform a consistent GCSE level Welsh, giving those starting it later, especially heavy hearted relative chances when applying for higher education study. Furthermore, Plaid Cymru advocates for introducing Welsh in different parts of the curriculum, including maths and science. There are around 700,000 Welsh speakers in Wales, which already outnumbers the population of many British towns and cities. Nonetheless, these numbers are distributed unevenly across the country, with the highest concentrations in the north-west, near the city of Bangor and in the south-west, where around half the population can converse in Welsh. To reach its target by 2050 and turn around the current stagnating trend, the party wants Welsh taught in all schools uniformly.
